The nineteen-hundred Paris Exposition Universelle was held from April through November and was the second major world's fair held in Paris, and indeed one of the largest expositions ever staged in human history. The fair welcomed over fifty million visitors from around the world and celebrated the dawn of the new century with Art Nouveau design, technological marvels, and the grandeur of the Belle Époque at its absolute peak. Officially, the fair celebrated the transition to the twentieth century and served as a showcase for French cultural and technological achievements to the world. One of its most important introductions was the Métropolitain, also known as the Paris Metro, a marvel of modern engineering that allowed efficient transport of fair visitors throughout the exposition grounds. What made this truly significant was that it became permanent infrastructure, fundamentally transforming how Parisians moved through their city for decades to come. The fairgrounds extended along both banks of the Seine River and utilised iconic structures including the Grand Palais and Petit Palais, permanent buildings that still stand today. The fair featured extensive Art Nouveau design and architecture throughout its spaces, establishing the aesthetic movement's visibility and influence across Europe and beyond. It displayed innovations in electricity, aviation, automotive design, and entertainment that exemplified fin-de-siècle optimism and confidence in technological progress. The fair marked the zenith of Paris's cultural dominance before World War I reshuffled European power dynamics and transformed the continent.
